transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05
Time: 2:00 PM PST
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Jade Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Anya Gomez (Redwood CSM briefly), Lena Ortiz (CTO, Quantum Retail), Markus Engel (ML Engineer), Priya Nair (Product), Samir Das (Infra)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, core params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff strategies, and brief mention of Console + Redwood Optimize recommendations for cost and latency. Customer is evaluating for a chat assistant and dynamic product copy generation; primary constraints: 50-100ms p50 latency targets for short prompts, cost sensitivity at scale, and SOC2/compliance for customer data.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API overview and quick curl/SDK examples
- Streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs
- Request parameters and best practices (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop tokens)
- Retries, idempotency, and backoff
- Basic Console demo (routes, usage dashboards) and Optimize suggestions (batching, cache)
- Next steps: POC benchmark and security docs

Action items (also in metadata): see above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jade Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jade with redwood inference, i run the east coast accounts - um - excited to walk through our hosted api and a couple of patterns we see for chat and text generation
[00:14] Lena Ortiz: thanks, jade - big picture first, we want to power a shopping assistant for our web app and also generate short product descriptions. our main thing is latency while keeping cost down, and security is non-negotiable - we are SOC2 in progress.
[00:28] Marcus Lee: great, that helps. quick question on current setup - markus, can you share the traffic profile?
[00:33] Markus Engel: we expect roughly 10k reqs/day initially, spiky, peak ~200 rps, payloads are short - typical user prompt is 50 tokens or less, and then we append context of 200 tokens. our target is p50 ~50-100ms for the assistant, p95 can be higher.
[00:51] Marcus Lee: ok got it. couple of things i'll demo: the hosted api call patterns, streaming output which helps perceived latency, and parameters that change output shape and cost. i may also show a tiny console screenshot later.
[01:03] Priya Nair: also curious about retries - we run a global load balancer and want safe retries without duplicating charges if a request actually went through.
[01:10] Marcus Lee: totally - we'll cover idempotency tokens and retry semantics. quick primer: for streaming we use server-sent events and you can start rendering tokens as they arrive; that reduces time-to-first-token dramatically versus waiting for the full response. but streaming does make retries trickier because once you started streaming you can't safely retry the same request without potential duplication unless you have idempotency at the application level.
[01:34] Samir Das: how do you recommend doing that? we have a user session id and message ids in our infra.
[01:38] Marcus Lee: perfect - attach an idempotency key tied to the message id in the header. if you get a network failure before you receive final status, you can check server side whether the message id completed or not. in hosted mode redwood stores short-lived request logs for this purpose when enabled; for strict guarantees you can use our dedicated or private deployments where you control the logs/ack semantics.
[01:58] Lena Ortiz: ok. can you show an example curl?
[02:02] Marcus Lee: sure - example, high level: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -H 'Idempotency-Key: <msg-id>' -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a 20-word product blurb for a running shoe"}], "stream":true, "temperature":0.2, "max_tokens":60 }' - you'll get an SSE stream back with tokens. (note: transcript may scramble some punctuation)
[02:34] Priya Nair: we do node frontends and would prefer SDK examples.
[02:37] Marcus Lee: our JS SDK has a streaming client where you can subscribe to token events; simple snippet will be in the follow-up. for most UIs we recommend streaming the assistant's tokens to show typing early, then finalize after the stream completes.
[02:52] Markus Engel: what's the cost delta for streaming vs non-streaming?
[02:55] Marcus Lee: no intrinsic cost delta - cost is per token generated either way. streaming just changes client experience and how you handle retries. however, you can combine streaming with prefix caching (we call it KV cache) to reduce tokens for repeated context; that reduces token usage and cost.
[03:14] Lena Ortiz: you mentioned parameters - what do you recommend for temperature and top_p for product copy vs chat?
[03:19] Marcus Lee: for deterministic copy we use low temp ~0.0-0.3 and occasionally top_p 0.9; for chat, temp 0.2-0.7 depending on desired creativity. max_tokens you should cap to avoid runaway costs; we support token limits per request and also per-route quotas in the Console.
[03:38] Jade Park: we also have automatic retries with exponential backoff in our official SDKs; default behavior is 3 retries with jitter, but you can tune that or disable it if your app handles idempotency.
[03:49] Samir Das: do you have guidance on retry timing?
[03:52] Marcus Lee: common pattern: short retry for 429s (rate limit) with backoff starting 200-500ms, and for 5xx you usually back off longer - 1s -> 4s -> 8s, etc. and always respect the Retry-After header if present. our Console exposes rate limit headers and per-route metrics so you can tune client-side backoffs based on observed quota.
[04:16] Priya Nair: how do we avoid partial duplicates if a stream fails mid-way?
[04:19] Marcus Lee: two approaches: 1) make the server-side idempotency authoritative and check on reconnect (requires request persistence), 2) do optimistic rendering on the client but store the last message id and reconcile once the final token arrives. we'll include a short doc in the follow-up illustrating both.
[04:36] Lena Ortiz: switching to observability - can we see per-route latency and per-token cost in the Console?
[04:40] Marcus Lee: yes - Console has route-level dashboards, token breakdowns, p50/p95 latency histograms, and cost per route. Redwood Optimize will also give you quantization and batching suggestions for large workloads. for example, if you have many short requests, Optimize may suggest smaller batch windows and more aggressive prefix cache settings.
[05:02] Markus Engel: curious about model selection - do you host open models and private models?
[05:06] Marcus Lee: we maintain a curated catalog of open models and provide performance profiles - latency/cost benchmarks. you can pin a model version per route. when capacity is constrained, smart routing can fall back to cheaper model variants; you can control fallback policies per-route.
[05:21] Priya Nair: security - KMS integration and how data is stored?
[05:25] Marcus Lee: hosted API stores transient request logs for debugging and idempotency unless customer opts out; we offer KMS integration for encryption at rest and can configure shorter retention. we have SOC2 reports and can share a security pack; for stricter controls you can choose Dedicated or Private where logs never leave customer VPC.
[05:44] Lena Ortiz: good. timeline - if we like the POC we want to go to production in Q1.
[05:48] Jade Park: perfect - let's align the POC to mimic your peak traffic and latency SLOs.
[05:53] Marcus Lee: i'll demo a quick SDK call now and then show the Console screenshot.
[05:58] Marcus Lee: (screen share) here's the JS snippet: client.chat.stream({ messages: [...], temperature: 0.2, stream: true }) .on('token', t => render(t)) .on('end', () => commit()) - again, simplified. we'll attach full snippets.
[06:22] Priya Nair: looking at rate limits - do you have per-route quotas we can increase for the POC?
[06:27] Jade Park: yes we can provision increased quota for the POC and bump after review; for enterprise accounts we also offer reserved capacity (dedicated) if predictable throughput is required.
[06:36] Markus Engel: about batching - will batching increase latency for individual short queries?
[06:40] Marcus Lee: batching trades off throughput vs per-request latency. for many short requests, we use micro-batching (sub-10ms aggregation) to keep latency low while improving GPU utilization. Optimize will recommend batching windows that fit your distribution. if strict p50 latency is critical, we can tune to minimal batching and complement with autoscaling of capacity.
[07:02] Lena Ortiz: ok - what's a reasonable POC to validate our two use-cases: the assistant and the copy generator?
[07:06] Marcus Lee: typical POC: 48-72 hours running your traffic profile with: routed hosted API endpoints, a mix of streaming and non-streaming calls, capture p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens. we'll run side-by-side baseline with your current provider if desired.
[07:21] Samir Das: will we need network peering or special firewall rules?
[07:24] Marcus Lee: for hosted api, usual outbound HTTPS is enough. if you prefer VPC peering for lower egress and private endpoints, that's available under Dedicated/Private. for the POC hosted mode we usually don't require peering.
[07:36] Jade Park: ok recap - we will: send pricing and security docs, Marcus will prepare a POC script and sample payloads, Markus to send traffic profile, and we'll schedule the POC next week.
[07:47] Lena Ortiz: sounds good, thanks.
[07:49] Marcus Lee: one last note on retry semantics: our SDK includes automatic retry for idempotent endpoints; for streaming endpoints the SDK defaults to surface partials and leaves retry to the app. we'll document patterns.
[08:03] Priya Nair: any caveats around function calling or structured output?
[08:07] Marcus Lee: we support structured outputs and function-like calls but that's more deterministic when you set low temperature and use stop tokens. function calling has similar retry considerations as streaming.
[08:18] Jade Park: thanks all, we'll follow up with the pack and scheduling.

End of call.
